summary: Defines a MIB module for managing implementations of Multicast Listener Discovery in IPv6, so network tools can read its status and settings. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 5519.

eli5.summary: This is a dashboard that lets people check how a computer keeps track of which group broadcasts it wants to hear. A newer document later replaced it.

questions: snmp objects for multicast listener discovery
how to manage multicast in ipv6 networks
subtitle: Management tools for IPv6 multicast group announcements

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to monitor and manage multicast group membership in IPv6 networks using Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD).
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module with two tables: one tracking MLD configuration per interface, and one tracking which IPv6 multicast groups have listeners on each interface.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can use SNMP to view MLD state and configure protocol parameters in IPv6 networks. RFC 5519 updated this to add MLD version 2 support.

today: RFC 3019 is a Proposed Standard for IPv6 MLD management. It was replaced by RFC 5519, which extended the MIB to cover MLD version 2 and added IPv6 multicast forwarding support.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) on IPv6 networks. MLD is described in RFC 2710 and is the IPv6 equivalent of IGMP for IPv4. The MIB allows network administrators to monitor and configure MLD on routers and hosts using SNMP.

MLD allows IPv6 hosts to announce they want to receive traffic sent to a particular multicast group address. Routers use MLD to discover which groups have listeners on each interface and forward multicast packets accordingly. This MIB exposes MLD state and configuration to management tools.
sections.eli5: IPv6 computers announce which group broadcasts they want to hear using MLD. Managers need a standard way to check and control this.

sections.title: MLD and IPv6 Multicast
sections.content:
IPv6 uses multicast addresses to send packets to multiple receivers. Unlike IPv4 broadcasting, which reaches all devices on a network, multicast allows selective delivery to only devices that have explicitly joined a group. MLD is the protocol hosts use to join and leave multicast groups, and routers use to learn which groups have members on each interface.

RFC 2710 defines MLD Version 1, a simple mechanism for group membership reporting. Without a standard MIB, administrators could not monitor MLD activity or adjust protocol parameters like query intervals or response timeouts. This RFC fills that gap for IPv6 networks, providing visibility and control over multicast group memberships.
sections.eli5: IPv6 broadcasts to specific groups instead of everyone. Managers need to see which computers joined which groups and tune the protocol.

sections.title: MIB Tables: Interface and Cache
sections.content:
The MIB module defines two main tables, mirroring the structure of the IGMP MIB for IPv4. The MLD Interface Table contains one row for each interface on which MLD is enabled. It tracks the MLD version, the IPv6 address of the current querier (the device sending membership queries), query timing parameters, and statistics on membership joins and group count. Key configuration objects include mldInterfaceQueryInterval (default 125 seconds) and mldInterfaceQueryMaxResponseDelay (default 10 seconds).

The MLD Cache Table contains one row for each IPv6 multicast group with members on a particular interface. Each row records whether the local system is a member, the IPv6 address of the host that last reported membership, when the entry was created, and when it will expire.
sections.eli5: One table tracks settings on each interface. Another lists IPv6 groups with listeners and when they expire.

sections.title: Configuration and Monitoring
sections.content:
The MIB allows administrators to enable or disable MLD on each interface using mldInterfaceStatus. The mldInterfaceVersion object is defined as a placeholder for future versions of MLD. The mldInterfaceQueryMaxResponseDelay allows tuning the maximum response time for group-specific queries. The mldInterfaceRobustness variable tunes for expected packet loss, allowing the protocol to be more resilient on lossy subnets. The mldInterfaceLastListenQueryIntvl controls leave latency by tuning group-specific query intervals.

Read-only monitoring objects track the IPv6 address of the current querier, how long it has held the role, when its term expires, the count of membership joins, and the current number of groups with members on the interface.
sections.eli5: Managers can turn MLD on or off, pick response times, adjust for packet loss, and control how quickly groups are cleaned up when members leave.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
Some MIB objects expose sensitive information about multicast group membership. The mldCacheSelf and mldCacheLastReporter objects can reveal which IPv6 addresses are listening to specific groups. Read-write and read-create objects allow administrators to configure MLD, and unauthorized changes could deny service by disrupting multicast delivery.

SNMPv1 provides no authentication or encryption. The RFC recommends using SNMPv3 with the User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control to restrict access to authorized administrators. Proper configuration of SNMP access control is essential to prevent unauthorized users from monitoring group memberships or disrupting multicast services by modifying MLD parameters.
sections.eli5: Knowing which computers listen to which groups reveals private information. Only trusted managers should be able to read group lists or change settings.
